manager_name: Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry
headline: Cutting migration dramatically would damage the Australian economy and worsen skills gaps in construction, tourism and trades, putting it 'in a hole which would be very hard to get out of'
reasoning: Andrew McKellar argues that framing the migration debate around a target number rather than skills needs is the wrong approach. He contends that extreme cuts such as One Nation's proposal to reduce migration by 750,000 would deprive sectors like construction and tourism of the labour they need. He notes the economy is already constrained around 2% growth and needs its speed limit raised, not lowered. He advocates a holistic approach combining investment in training, increased workforce participation, and targeted migration to fill remaining gaps.
quote: The critical question that we should be asking is how do we cover the skills gaps that we have? How do we ensure that we can prime the economy to grow at the, you know, fastest rate possible? And how do we ensure that the benefits of that growth are spread across the existing population. Now, the question that one nation are asking doesn't go to any of those points. They're really starting at with an arbitrary figure. They're talking about cutting in a very extreme way and that'll end up with far reaching damage to the Australian economy. It'll mean that sectors like construction and tourism and areas like that are not going to be able to get the skilled people, the labour that they need and it would put the economy in a hole which would be very hard to get out of.
episode_title: Can Australia really migrate its way out of a skills gap?

manager_name: Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry
headline: Apprenticeship commencements falling, fee-free TAFE insufficient as 60%+ of VET occurs outside TAFE in private providers not receiving equivalent benefits; Skilling Australia Fund levy not being recycled into training effectively
reasoning: McKellar highlights that apprenticeship commencements are declining, which will not help solve the skills gap. He points out that fee-free TAFE is only a partial solution because more than 60% of vocational education and training occurs in private sector institutions and colleges that do not receive the same benefits. He also notes that the Skilling Australia Fund levy paid by employers when hiring migrants is not being returned to training to the full extent needed, representing a missed opportunity to fund skills development.
quote: At the moment, apprenticeship commencements are going backwards. That's not going to help solve the issue. We've got, you know, fee free TAFE, that's all very well, but that is not providing the full solution because more than 60% of all vocational education and training takes place outside of TAFE in private sector institutions and colleges and private training providers. They're not getting the same benefits. So we have to boost that investment. There are sources that we can draw on to do that and some of them come from migrants and some of them come when we bring migrants in. Employers have to pay a Skilling Australia fund levy. That's not going back into training to the full extent, so we need to ensure that we're getting that money where it needs to go.
episode_title: Can Australia really migrate its way out of a skills gap?

manager_name: Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry
headline: AI safety requires both Australian and global standards; uncontrolled development risks loss of community confidence and undermines the technology's economic benefits
reasoning: McKellar acknowledged that warnings from people close to AI development about slowing down deserve careful attention. He agrees that standards and safeguards are necessary and that these cannot be confined to Australia alone but must be implemented globally. He warns that if AI development proceeds in a completely uncontrolled way, community confidence in the technology could be lost, which would undermine the economic opportunities it offers.
quote: I think it's a timely warning that's coming from some of those people who are very close to the development of this technology. And so we listen carefully to those points of view. We agree there need to be some standards and some safeguards in place. You know, that can't just occur in Australia. We've got to see that happening around the world. But you know, AI safety is a huge issue. It's a huge challenge. If we don't address it properly and comprehensively, you know, then the risk is that we will lose community confidence in the opportunities that that technology offers. So, you know, we agreed there's a place for Australian standards, there's a place for global standards on this.
episode_title: Can Australia really migrate its way out of a skills gap?
